item.title: Reading, Hearing and Keeping the Word
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: Most people avoid Revelation because it feels too strange, too dangerous, too easy to get wrong. In Revelation 1:1–3, the book opens not with a warning but with a promise — a specific blessing for anyone who reads, hears, and holds on to what is written. This sermon unpacks what that blessing actually means: not a passive exposure to information, but the kind of hearing that says "I want that," and the kind of keeping that looks like carrying on with your homework while the plane flies through the storm. If you have ever picked up Revelation and put it back down, this is a good place to start.

item.title: Jerusalem Receives the Lion of Judah
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: You are living in the gap between Pentecost and the return of Christ. The question is not whether history is moving toward something — it clearly is. The question is what you are building while you wait, and whether it will still be standing when the Lion of Judah arrives.
item.content:encoded: You are living in the gap between Pentecost and the return of Christ. The question is not whether history is moving toward something — it clearly is. The question is what you are building while you wait, and whether it will still be standing when the Lion of Judah arrives.
item.itunes:author: Peter Stoffberg
item.itunes:subtitle: History has a destination. The only question is what you are building before it gets there.
item.itunes:summary: You are somewhere in the middle — past the beginning, not yet at the end — and the question is what you are doing with that space. Joel 2 splits down the middle: one half already fulfilled on the day of Pentecost, one half still coming, and right now you are living in the gap between them. This sermon traces that gap through three sites — a Roman hippodrome where Christians knelt in gravel sand and died rather than deny what they believed, ancient temple steps where a small crowd sang louder than every mosque in Jerusalem, and the Mount of Olives where every prophecy from Joel to Zechariah to Revelation converges on a single return. What you will find here is a concrete and uncomfortable question: are you building something that lasts, or something that impresses? If you are wondering whether any of it matters, or whether you have the time, this is for you.

item.title: Jerusalem Rejects the Lamb of God
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: A first-hand visit to Jerusalem — the torture chamber in Caiaphas' house, the garden tomb, the Mount of Olives — and what happens to your faith when the archaeology keeps agreeing with the text.
item.content:encoded: A first-hand visit to Jerusalem — the torture chamber in Caiaphas' house, the garden tomb, the Mount of Olives — and what happens to your faith when the archaeology keeps agreeing with the text.
item.itunes:author: Peter Stoffberg
item.itunes:subtitle: What Jerusalem looks like in person, and why it makes the Bible harder to ignore.
item.itunes:summary: Standing inside Caiaphas' house — the high priest who ordered Jesus' arrest — and finding the torture pillars still in the rock, leather still threaded through the holes, is the kind of thing that stops you mid-sentence. This sermon follows a visit to Jerusalem: the Church of the Holy Sepulchre with its 300-year argument over a ladder, the garden tomb where every detail of the resurrection accounts lines up with the archaeology, and the Mount of Olives where a geological fault sits exactly where Zechariah said it would. The question it keeps returning to is why, with all of that sitting in stone, we still treat our Bibles like they might be negotiable.

item.title: When in Rome
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: You've probably used "when in Rome" as a reason to lower your standards — most people have. But when Paul arrived in Rome under house arrest, chained to a soldier and cut off from everything that made his ministry work, he didn't renegotiate his convictions. He renegotiated his methods. Acts 28 shows a man who couldn't go to the synagogue, so he brought the synagogue to him — and then preached from morning until evening to whoever came. The difference the passage draws is precise: circumstances change, obedience doesn't. If your Rome right now is a health crisis, a job situation, or a family corner you've been backed into, this is for you.

item.title: Evidence for Christianity
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: The shipwreck account in Acts 28 is one of the most archaeologically verified passages in the New Testament. The depths, the geography, the anchors — it all checks out. If the facts hold, what does that mean for the parts you can't verify?
item.content:encoded: The shipwreck account in Acts 28 is one of the most archaeologically verified passages in the New Testament. The depths, the geography, the anchors — it all checks out. If the facts hold, what does that mean for the parts you can't verify?
item.itunes:author: Peter Stoffberg
item.itunes:subtitle: Before you decide what to believe, here is what the archaeology actually says.
item.itunes:summary: If you've ever quietly wondered whether faith is just a choice you make despite the evidence, Acts 28 pushes back on that. The account of Paul's shipwreck on Malta — the water depths, the geography, the anchors still being dug up from that bay, the title of the island's governor — has been cross-checked against archaeology, oceanography, and ancient records, and it holds. Acts 28:1–10 makes the case that if Luke got the mundane facts exactly right, the parts that can't be dug up or carbon-dated deserve the same serious hearing. For anyone sitting with doubt rather than certainty, this is a fair place to start.
item.itunes:title: Evidence for Christianity

item.title: Shipwrecked or Rescued?
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: Prolonged suffering is nobody’s desire. Nobody wants to be endure dark, cold, painful suffering. Nobody wants to be shipwrecked, we all want to be rescued. But what if the shipwreck is our rescue? Paul’s arrival in Malta ends weeks of suffering, but it also testifies to God’s grace and power. 275 people were given a once in a lifetime opportunity to know God and His goodness. That’s something far more valuable than a ship, it’s cargo and even the mortal lives of those on board. God can use shipwrecks to rescue us.

item.title: Carried Along
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: Paul’s voyage to Rome shows how Jesus Christ upholds the universe with His powerful Word. Storms are an apt metaphor for life. They can arise suddenly and can take us to the point of losing all hope, but they can do something else. Coming to the end of ourselves delivers us to the foot of the cross, where we can truly begin to trust in the Lord with all our hearts. This is a great gift and powerful liberation. The bumpier the road, the more obvious it becomes that Jesus is actually carrying us, not being a crutch.

item.title: Freedom
item.dc:creator: Peter
item.description: We all long for freedom. So many things promise it, or some form or concept of it. But true freedom is not what it’s sold as. Freedom is not just being able to do what we want, more importantly, it’s the freedom of not having to do what we want. We don;t always want to do the right thing, or what is best for us and those we love. The compulsion to do what is bad for us and those around us is sin, and it’s consequence is ultimately death. The only freedom from this comes by faith in Christ Jesus and the subsequent work of the Holy Spirit of God. Paul’s time with some of the most powerful and popular leaders proves this irony and gives us, and those we get to share it with, a chance for real freedom.

Freedom is not just being able to do what we want, more importantly, it’s the freedom of not having to do what we want. We don;t always want to do the right thing, or what is best for us and those we love. The compulsion to do what is bad for us and those around us is sin, and it’s consequence is ultimately death. The only freedom from this comes by faith in Christ Jesus and the subsequent work of the Holy Spirit of God. Paul’s time with some of the most powerful and popular leaders proves this irony and gives us, and those we get to share it with, a chance for real freedom.
